title: (title unknown)
bodyHtml:
Computers, like humans, often encounter words they have never seen before among the stream of language constantly inundating them, which can pose a challenge for the computer's understanding of language. One approach for handling novel words is to use a character-level model of language: Whereas word-level models treat words as non-decomposable units, character-level models can learn how individual letters (or chunks of letters) work together to create word meaning. For example, if a character-level model encounters the novel word non-walruslike, it could figure out its meaning based on the meanings of smaller chunks (non-, walrus, and like).

However, such a model might make mistakes if it breaks the word down incorrectly. The table on the left shows a list of words that a hypothetical character-level model might interpret incorrectly, while the table on the right shows (in random order) the definitions it might generate.

questions.partPrompt: What English words would the model give the following definitions? Hint: One of these three words appears in the word list above.

questions.promptHtml: C. not not going out with

hints.text: Forget what each word really means. Instead, look for smaller words and familiar word-parts hiding inside the letters: the model chops the string wherever it recognizes something, even in the wrong place.

Two kinds of chunk show up. Some are real prefixes and suffixes used with the wrong meaning (like re- for "again", de- for "remove", pre- for "before", -ess for "female", -y for "like", -ling for "small"), and some are whole ordinary words that happen to be spelled inside the longer word. Match a definition by translating its parts back into chunks and then gluing the chunks together.

Try the method on a word that is not in the puzzle: carpet. A character-level model could split it as car + pet and define it as "animal companion belonging to a vehicle". Notice how the definition names each chunk in order. Read each definition in the right-hand table the same way, chunk by chunk, and count the syllables you would need.

explanationHtml:
What the "model" is doing

A character-level model does not memorize whole words. It looks at the letters and tries to recognize familiar pieces: prefixes (bits added to the front, like re- or pre-), suffixes (bits added to the end, like -ess or -y) and ordinary words. Then it adds the meanings of those pieces together. That works nicely for a made-up word like non-walruslike, but it goes wrong when the letters of an ordinary word accidentally contain pieces that have nothing to do with its real meaning.

Strategy

For each definition, translate its wording back into pieces and then ask which word on the left is spelled out by those pieces in that order. Useful equivalences to keep in mind:

  • "again / once more" = re-; "beforehand" = pre-; "remove" = de-; "not" = in- or un-; "in favor of" = pro-; "sharing the role of" = co-; "former" = ex-
  • "one" = uni-; "two" = bi-; "three" = tri-
  • "female" = -ess; "small" = -ling or wee; "like" = -y; "group of" = list; "era" = age

Worked examples

conundrum: the definition talks about something "sharing the role of" (co-) a "beaten instrument" (drum) used by "female religious figures" (nun). Put them in the order the definition gives them and you get co + nun + drum.

divergent: "courteous man" is a gent, and someone "who descends below water" is a diver: diver + gent.

puffiness: a "northern bird" is a puffin, and "female" is the suffix -ess. The model reads the real suffix -ness as -ess attached to puffin.

properties: "appropriate" is proper and "pieces of neckwear" are ties, so the model splits the word after proper.

Notice how the definitions are careful to name the chunks in the same order as the letters. That ordering is your best checking tool: if a definition's parts come out in the wrong order for a candidate word, the match is wrong.

Part G2: going backwards

Here you build the word yourself from the pieces the definition names. "Having two..." starts with bi-, and the plural of "male child" gives you the rest. "Did hurt once more" needs "once more" (re-) plus a past-tense form meaning "did hurt". For C, "not not" means two negative prefixes stacked up, followed by a word for "going out with" in its -ing form. The hint that one of the three answers appears earlier in the problem points you to the very first paragraph of the introduction, where one long word happens to begin with two negative-looking prefixes.

Why linguists care

This is a joke version of a real problem in natural language processing. Systems that split words into sub-word units (such as byte-pair encoding, used by many modern language models) genuinely do carve mistrust into pieces, and nothing stops the pieces from being mist and rust. Human readers use context and knowledge of real morphology (the study of how words are built from meaningful parts) to avoid these traps; a purely letter-based system has to learn to as well.
